newsitem.title: UK: UK PMI unlikely to provoke Feb rate rise-analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK PMI unlikely to provoke Feb rate rise-analysts.

text.p: A hefty rise in the UK purchasing managers' index in January will add weight to the argument for tighter monetary policy to contain consumer-led price pressure.

But with an election looming, economists say Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is likely to stand firm against any calls for a rate rise at his meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
"Ahead of the election, the government will not be worried by pound strength if it helps to justify keeping base rates at six percent," said Jeremy Hawkins at Bank America in London.
The PMI index rose to 54.0 in January after staging a sharp decline to 52.8 in December.The survey showed the first rise in the pace of manufacturing growth since last October.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS), which conducted the survey, said the improvement in the PMI was driven by a rise in the rate of growth of new orders, due largely to rising domestic demand for consumer goods.
"Generally speaking, the survey was more healthy than had been expected," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
Analysts said the pattern of this month's survey, in which weakness in exports was effectively cancelled out by healthy consumer demand, was likely to continue throughout the year.
This, they said, poured some cold water on Clarke's argument that sterling's recent strength would be enough to contain upward pressure on consumer price inflation.
"Orders and output were both particularly robust last month and should bolster expectations that a rate hike is just a matter of time," said Hawkins.
But for this month at least, analysts said the Chancellor, anxious not to raise rates before the country goes to the polls by May 22, was likely to reject calls from George to raise rates.

"We are sceptical, like the Bank of England, of using sterling's strength as an excuse for not raising rates," said Cole. "But having said that, I think the Chancellor will use it as an excuse at this meeting."
George said at the December 11 monetary meeting that he might have to recommend a half-point increase in official rates in January or February.
But Clarke said at the weekend in Davos that he believed recent data had gone his way and justified his decision not to raise rates in December.
David Coleman, UK economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London, said interest rate markets could draw some comfort from the January survey.

While noting significant rises in output and new orders for the month, Coleman said the prices index, which eased back to 41.6 from 42.3 previously, would calm fears of an imminent tightening of monetary policy.

"Prices remain very subdued. The fall in January was the largest since last August and the survey again highlighted downward pressure on import pressure on import from the rise in sterling," Coleman said.
"Solid growth with little inflation -- it could almost be the U.S. economy."
Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets said the PMI survey was a touch stronger than expected and should help to allay fears that manufacturing could be heading back towards recession.

"But with the recovery in industry still fragile and costs pressures still very subdued, the report is most unlikely to prompt Mr Clarke to raise interest rates at Wednesday's monetary meeting," he said.
